signals.source_text: eVTOL 2035: Ten Assumptions That Could Break an eVTOL Business Case The most dangerous eVTOL assumptions are not the absurd ones. They are the reasonable ones that become wrong when several move against you at the same time. A programme can have a credible aircraft, serious certification progress and strong capital behind it, and still produce a weak route. Range can shrink once reserves, weather and battery ageing are taken into account. A vertiport can be ready while the grid is not. Weather can protect safety yet quietly destroy utilisation. Autonomy can arrive later than the economics assume it will. Insurance and residual value can take years of operating evidence to mature. The bigger risk is correlation: weak demand reduces the load factor, low utilisation spreads fixed costs across fewer sectors, degraded battery performance compresses mission capability, and infrastructure delays strand capital. That is why the real eVTOL question is no longer simply: Can the aircraft fly, or even be certified? It is: Can the complete operating system remain dependable, financeable and scalable when several assumptions become adverse together? My new article examines 10 assumptions that should be treated as evidence gates rather than planning defaults. It draws on eVTOL 2035 — The Global Built-World Intelligence Reference, a 72-page decision framework that connects aircraft, infrastructure, energy, operations, economics, insurance, autonomy, data, and public Legitimacy. The free six-page Executive Preview and named-user licences are available now: https://lnkd.in/dWHueUqA #eVTOL #AdvancedAirMobility #Aviation #AviationFinance #Infrastructure https://lnkd.in/dVPNisVs
